Q1(a): Define Data Structure. Explain primitive and non-primitive data structures with classification diagram and memory allocation principles.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 1]:
A data structure is a specialized format for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data in computer memory efficiently.
• Primitive Data Structures: Int (4 bytes), Float (4 bytes), Char (1 byte), Double (8 bytes), Pointer.
• Non-Primitive Data Structures:
  - Linear: Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists (sequential layout).
  - Non-Linear: Trees, Graphs (hierarchical layout).
• Memory Allocation: Static allocation uses stack memory at compile-time. Dynamic allocation uses heap memory at runtime via pointers.

Q1(a) [Primitive & Non-Primitive Data Structures]:

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 1]:
Primitive data structures: The data structures that are directly operated upon by machine level instructions, i.e. fundamental data types such as int, float, char, double.
• Non-Primitive Data Structures:
  - Linear: Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists
  - Non-Linear: Trees, Graphs

Q1(a) [Continuation from Page 1 - Non-Primitive Classification & Data Structure Operations]:

• In a linear data structure, the data items are arranged in a linear order or sequential.
  Eg. array, stack, list, queue

  Eg. trees and graphs

1b) It is a fundamental problem in computer science where the goal is find all occurrences of a given pattern within a larger text or string.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 2 (Starting at 1b))]:
• Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm is a string-matching algorithm that eliminates backtracking by preprocessing the pattern to construct a prefix/failure function π table.
• Algorithm Logic: On mismatch at character P[q], shift pattern index to π[q-1] to skip redundant comparisons.

Q4(a): Explain Circular Queue with enqueue() and dequeue() operations and wrap-around condition.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 4]:
Circular Queue overcomes memory wastage of linear queues by wrapping around using modulo arithmetic.

Matching Phase: Searching P in Text T = "abxababaca". Match found starting at index 4 in O(n + m) time complexity.

Q5(a): Define Binary Tree. Write recursive algorithms for Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder traversals.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 5]:
A Binary Tree is a hierarchical non-linear data structure where each node has at most two children (left and right).
• Inorder (Left, Root, Right): inorder(root->left); printf("%d ", root->val); inorder(root->right);

Q5(b): Binary Search Tree (BST) operations: Insert, Search, and Delete.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 5]:
• Insert: If val < root->data, recurse left; if val > root->data, recurse right.
• Search: Time complexity O(h). If key == root->data return found.

Q9(a): Define Graph Data Structure. Explain Graph representations using Adjacency Matrix and Adjacency List with examples and memory comparison.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 6]:
A Graph G = (V, E) is a non-linear data structure consisting of vertices V and edges E connecting pairs of vertices.
• Adjacency Matrix: V x V 2D array representation. Fast O(1) edge lookup, but O(V²) space complexity.
• Adjacency List: Array of linked lists representing adjacent vertices. O(V + E) space complexity; efficient for sparse graphs.
• Graph Traversals: BFS uses Queue (level-order traversal); DFS uses Stack / Recursion (path discovery).

Q7(a): Define Heap and Priority Queue. Explain Max-Heap and Min-Heap with array representation and heapify algorithm.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 7]:
A Heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property.
• Max-Heap: Every parent node >= children nodes. Root has maximum element.
• Min-Heap: Every parent node <= children nodes. Root has minimum element.
• Array Representation: Parent at (i-1)/2, Left Child at 2i+1, Right Child at 2i+2.
• Heapify: Restores heap property downwards in O(log n) time.

Q7(b): Explain construction of Binary Search Tree and Height Balanced AVL Trees.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 7]:
• BST Property: Left subtree keys < Root key < Right subtree keys.
• AVL Trees: Self-balancing BST with Balance Factor = Height(Left) - Height(Right) in {-1, 0, 1}.
• Rotations: LL, RR, LR, RL single and double rotations maintain O(log n) search time.

Q8(a): Explain Hashing and Collision Resolution Techniques: Separate Chaining vs Open Addressing.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 8]:
Hashing maps large key values to small array indices using hash function h(key).
• Collision Handling:
  1. Separate Chaining: Each hash slot is a linked list of collided keys.
  2. Open Addressing: All elements stored directly in hash table. Probing methods: Linear Probing ((h(k) + i) % m), Quadratic Probing, Double Hashing.

Q8(b): Explain Hash Functions (Division, Multiplication, Mid-Square) and Load Factor α.

[Student Hand-Written Response - Page 8]:
• Division Method: h(k) = k mod m (where m is prime).
• Multiplication Method: h(k) = floor(m * (k * A mod 1)) where A ≈ 0.618.
• Mid-Square Method: Square key k, extract middle r bits.
• Load Factor: α = n / m (ratio of stored keys to table size).
